summary: A proposal to remove the 30-second delay the IMP imposes before accepting input from a Host that has just come up. The delay lets the news that the Host is up spread through the network. It explains why the delay existed and how the aim could be met in another way.

plainLanguage.summary: A rule makes new computers wait half a minute so everyone hears they are back. This note suggests a smarter way so nobody has to wait.

questions: imp 30 second delay host comes up
subtitle: Removing network startup delay for hosts on ARPANET

tldr.problem: When a host comes up on ARPANET, the IMP waits 30 seconds before accepting input, to ensure all IMPs in the network have learned the host is online.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of detecting dead destinations at the source IMP, the proposal moves that detection to the destination IMP, which instantly knows when its own hosts are online.
tldr.outcome: Hosts no longer wait for the worst-case network propagation delay; they can send messages immediately when ready.

today: RFC 410 was issued in November 1972 as a proposal to modify ARPANET behavior. It was neither deprecated nor updated; the change it proposed was a technical operational matter.

sections.title: The 30-Second Startup Delay
sections.content: When a host comes up on ARPANET, the IMP (Interface Message Processor, the network switch) currently waits 30 seconds before accepting input from that host. This delay exists to let news of the host's return spread through the network so all IMPs can update their tables of which hosts are up or down. The problem arises because if a host sends a message before a distant IMP knows it is online, that IMP will reject the reply as going to a dead destination.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer has to wait before the network knows it is awake, like waiting for a phone system to register that your phone has been turned back on.

sections.title: Why the Current Scheme Causes Problems
sections.content: The 30-second delay is set to the worst-case time for routing information to spread through the network topology. Three drawbacks exist: hosts at the same IMP or nearby do not need this full delay; the delay complicates half-duplex interfaces; and the timeout depends on network topology, making it hard to change if the network expands.
sections.plainLanguage: The 30 seconds is the longest possible wait, but many hosts should not have to wait that long. It also makes some equipment harder to use and makes it tricky to adjust the network later.

sections.title: A Better Way: Destination-Side Detection
sections.content: The proposal moves host dead-detection from the source IMP to the destination IMP. A destination IMP knows instantly when its own hosts come up because they are directly connected; it can immediately decide whether to hand a message to a host or send a destination dead error back to the source. Under this scheme, the host simply brings up its ready line and the IMP accepts input without delay.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of waiting for distant news, the receiving computer checks directly whether the target host is awake, like calling a house to see if someone is home instead of checking a written list.

sections.title: Effects on Hosts and Users
sections.content: Host software needs no changes; the host can attempt to send as soon as it brings up its ready line or delay as long as it wishes. The IMP will accept the message either way. Hosts may wish to remove any startup delays they have programmed in, as they are no longer necessary. Destination dead messages will now travel through the network before returning to the source, introducing more delay in error reporting and possibly arriving out of order if many messages go to the same dead host.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs do not need to change, but they could remove their own waiting periods if they had them. Error messages now have to travel farther but arrive less predictably.
